analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration and class action waivers in employee retirement and benefit plans.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, never received a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the nation's main private pension and benefit law (ERISA) to make forced arbitration clauses, class action waivers, and 'discretionary' clauses unenforceable in employee benefit plans. Workers and retirees could sue in court, join together in group claims, and get a fresh review of denied benefits instead of being pushed into private arbitration with rules written by their employer. It was introduced late in the session, attracted no cosponsors, and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees covered by employer benefit plans who would otherwise be locked out of court: they could bring claims under ERISA in court, join class or collective claims, refuse arbitration without retaliation, and get an independent judge to review denied benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees in benefit plans

how_it_helps.text: Renders mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses in employee benefit plans unenforceable, so workers and retirees can take benefit disputes to court instead of private arbitration [S3].

Allows voluntary post-dispute arbitration only under strict conditions: no coercion or threat of adverse action, a plain-language notice, a waiting period of at least 45 days, and written consent [S3].
Invalidates pre-dispute waivers of class, collective, and representative claims, so plan participants can join together in a single lawsuit rather than suing one by one [S3].

Strikes 'discretionary' clauses that give plan administrators power to interpret plan terms, requiring courts to review denied benefits fresh (de novo) rather than deferring to the administrator's own decision [S3].
Prohibits employers, plan sponsors, and plan administrators from requiring these provisions as a condition of participating in a plan or receiving benefits [S3].
Applies to disputes arising after enactment even where plan documents have not yet been updated, with a one-year grace period only for document updates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, plan sponsors, and benefit plan administrators, who would face more lawsuits and lose the tools (forced arbitration, class waivers, deference to their own benefit decisions) that limit their liability in disputes over benefits.

drawbacks.text: Defenders of arbitration argue it can resolve disputes faster and cheaper than court litigation; the bill would move many benefit claims into the courts, which can be slower and more expensive in individual cases [S3].
The bill covers only benefit-plan claims under ERISA; it does not touch forced arbitration in other employment disputes, such as wage or discrimination claims [S2].
The effective date reaches back over existing plan documents immediately for new disputes, which could produce a surge of litigation over older claims as soon as the law took effect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and retirees, the upside is substantial: it restores their day in court and the ability to band together when a plan shortchanges them, at a real cost to employers and administrators in litigation exposure. The main honest trade-off is that some individual disputes might move more slowly through court than through arbitration, and the bill leaves forced arbitration untouched in non-benefit employment disputes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never considered it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark DeSaulnier introduced the bill on May 12, 2022, less than eight months before the end of the 117th Congress [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day and received no further action [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, plan sponsors, and retirement plan administrators keep the forced arbitration clauses, class action waivers, and deference standards that limit their liability in benefit disputes, and arbitration providers keep the business those clauses generate.

for.name: Rep. Mark DeSaulnier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Committee on Education and Labor

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never held a markup or vote on the bill

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition.

industries.industry: Employers and employee benefit plan sponsors
industries.note: The bill strips their ability to require arbitration and class waivers as a condition of plan participation, exposing them to court and group lawsuits over benefits. Those tools exist to limit employer liability in exactly the disputes workers would bring [S3].
The bill voids 'discretionary' clauses and requires courts to review denied benefits fresh, removing the deference administrators currently get when they deny a claim [S3].
Banning mandatory pre-dispute arbitration in ERISA plans eliminates a large stream of forced-arbitration business tied to employee benefit disputes [S3].
